title: Introduction to the Second Law of Thermodynamics

children.text: Among the many capabilities of chemistry is its ability to predict if a process will occur under specified conditions. Thermodynamics, the study of relationships between the energy and work associated with chemical and physical processes, provides this predictive ability. Previous modules described various applications of thermochemistry, an important aspect of thermodynamics concerned with energy conservation. We used the conservation of energy to make predictions regarding the heat flow between hot and cold objects, and the heat flow accompanying chemical reactions and phase transitions. Conservation of energy allowed us to say, for example, that any energy leaving a hot metal bar must be equal to the energy that enters the water surrounding that bar. This conservation of energy is a consequence of the first law of thermodynamics. In this module, we will introduce additional thermodynamic concepts related to the second law of thermodynamics. The second law enables us to predict whether a chemical or physical changes will occur spontaneously at a given set of conditions.

The second law of thermodyamics indicates that the disorder of the universe is ever increasing and any process that occurs spontaneously contributes to this ever increasing disorder. If a reaction does not contribute to the increasing disorder of the universe, it will not occur spontaneously. Before we explore the details of the second law of thermodynamics we must first discuss the concepts of spontaneity and disorder.
